reason: The pancreatic islet cells are positioned to sense the glucose-rich blood after the meal.
expectation: The sensing cells will respond to the elevated glucose, likely by releasing insulin.

effect: The glucose-rich blood first had to be associated with the whole body; I can now try the pancreatic sensing cells.
reaction: The automatic compatibility feedback clarified the intended sequence.
reason: The pancreatic cells can now respond to the rising blood glucose in the body.
expectation: The pancreatic cells will detect rising glucose and release insulin.

effect: Rising glucose prompted pancreatic beta cells to release insulin into blood, with routes toward muscle and liver.
reaction: The inset makes the signal's origin and destinations clear.
reason: Insulin is shown travelling toward muscle, so the available skeletal muscle is a plausible next target.
expectation: Insulin will promote glucose uptake by muscle.

alternatives.reason: The liver is another indicated insulin target.

effect: Insulin-supported muscle uptake completed the post-meal goal; the focus is now maintaining blood glucose between meals.
reaction: The later inset clearly shows insulin release easing as blood glucose falls.
reason: The clock represents the shift to the between-meal period, when incoming glucose tapers.

choice.combine: Body taking up glucose into muscle

expectation: The body will move into a between-meal state with less glucose arriving from the gut.

effect: The between-meal interval lowered blood glucose while liver glycogen remains available.
reaction: The retained glycogen suggests a possible source of glucose.
reason: Pancreatic sensing cells include alpha cells, which can respond to falling blood glucose.
expectation: The alpha cells will release glucagon, signalling the liver to make glucose available.

alternatives.reason: The liver contains the stored glycogen, but a signal may be needed first.

effect: Falling blood glucose prompted alpha cells to release glucagon, which travels toward the liver.
reaction: The contrast with the earlier insulin response makes the two signals easier to follow.
reason: The liver contains glycogen and is the indicated target of glucagon.
expectation: Glucagon will prompt the liver to break down glycogen and release glucose into the blood.

effect: The liver released glucose from glycogen, and the subsequent reduction in glucagon illustrated feedback. Both chapter goals are complete.
reaction: The sequential insets brought the between-meal response together clearly.

mostWorthwhile.text: Following falling glucose through glucagon release to liver glycogen breakdown was worthwhile: the planned insets connect the signal, its target and the resulting feedback.

leastWorthwhile.text: The initial attempt was less worthwhile because the blood had to be combined with the whole body before the pancreatic cells could respond, although compatibility feedback resolved it automatically.

surprise.text: The first attempt instead attached the glucose-rich blood to the body; I had expected the pancreatic response immediately.

arbitrary.text: That required ordering felt somewhat artificial: the blood and pancreatic cells were already visually linked to the same body, so the need for an intermediate body state was not obvious.

continue.text: I would choose to continue if another chapter offered similarly clear physiological connections, though this chapter's largely predictable sequence left limited room for decisions.
